title: Classical Chinese I
tagline: What classical Chinese is, dictionaries and reference tools, content words and changes of meaning, function words, word-class shifts, word order and special patterns, phonetic loans and variant characters, punctuating classical texts, translating into modern Chinese, and reading whole texts
summary: Classical Chinese, the written language of more than two thousand years, is close enough to modern Chinese to look familiar and far enough to be misread. This course teaches the essentials of reading it: how words and their meanings differ from today, the common function words, word-class shifts, word order and special sentence patterns, phonetic loans, how to punctuate an unpunctuated text and how to translate accurately into modern Chinese, using passages from the standard classics.
overview: Classical Chinese (文言) is one of history's longest-lived written standards: born from the speech of the Eastern Zhou, frozen and renewed by two thousand years of imitation, and retired as a living medium only a century ago. This course teaches it as a language — with its own grammar, its own vocabulary, its own tools — not as a museum of moral quotations.

We build the workshop in the order a reader actually needs: what 文言 is and why it diverged from speech; the reference shelf (Shuowen, Kangxi, modern dictionaries, commentaries); content-word semantics (走, 去, 汤); the ten most profitable function words (之其而于为乃则者所); word-class shifts (noun used as verb, causative, putative); special orders (判断句, 宾语前置, 被动, 省略); phonetic loans and old/new character forms; punctuating unpunctuated texts; the eight techniques of translation; and finally sustained reading of complete passages from the Zuo Zhuan, the Analects, Mencius, Zhuangzi, and the prose of the eight masters.
No prerequisites; shares its sound-and-reading ledger with the phonology course. On completion you are ready for Classical Chinese II and the pre-Qin literature course.
outcomes: explain the classical/vernacular split as a diglossia and date its two-thousand-year arc
use Shuowen Jiezi, Kangxi Dictionary, Modern Chinese Dictionary and 古注/注释 to settle a word's sense
trace the semantic history of core content words (走/跑, 去, 汤, 臭, 牺牲, 江河) and date senses to periods
assign the main functions of 之 其 而 以 于 为 乃 则 者 所 in running text
recognise and translate noun-as-verb, causative and putative uses, and adjectival nouns used as adverbs
identify judgement sentences, passives, fronted objects, post-modifiers and ellipsis, and restore them to modern order
distinguish phonetic loans (通假) from old/later and variant graphs, and read them without being fooled
punctuate (句读) a lightly glossed classical text and translate it with the keep/replace/supply/delete rules

chapters.title: What classical Chinese is
chapters.summary: Classical Chinese and the vernacular, how the written language stayed stable for two millennia while speech changed, and why it is still worth reading.

chapters.title: Dictionaries and reference tools
chapters.summary: The *Shuowen Jiezi*, the *Kangxi Dictionary*, the *Ciyuan*, the *Hanyu Da Cidian* and dictionaries of common classical characters, and digital databases.

chapters.title: Content words and changes of meaning
chapters.summary: How meanings widened, narrowed or shifted (走 once meant ‘run’, 去 ‘leave’), how single-syllable words became compounds, and false friends between classical and modern Chinese.

chapters.title: Function words
chapters.summary: 之, 其, 而, 以, 于, 为, 乃, 则, 者 and 所: their uses and how to translate them.

chapters.title: Word-class shifts
chapters.summary: Nouns used as verbs, causative and putative uses, and nouns used as adverbials.

chapters.title: Word order and special sentence patterns
chapters.summary: Judgement sentences, passive constructions, fronted objects, postposed modifiers and omission.

chapters.title: Phonetic loans and variant characters
chapters.summary: Characters borrowed for their sound, earlier and later forms of one word, and variant forms, and how to tell them apart.

chapters.title: Punctuating classical texts
chapters.summary: Reading texts printed without punctuation, the clues that mark where sentences end, and classic mistakes of punctuation.

chapters.title: Translating into modern Chinese
chapters.summary: Literal and free translation, keeping, replacing, supplying, deleting and reordering words, and the standard of faithfulness, clarity and elegance.

chapters.title: Reading whole texts
chapters.summary: Close reading of complete passages from the *Zuo Zhuan*, the *Analects*, the *Mencius* and the *Zhuangzi*, using everything in the course.

history.title: The oracle-bone line begins
history.detail: Shang divination graphs and Zhou bronzes set the written language on its own track: brief, formulaic, unbothered by speech — the deep ancestry of 文言's concision.

history.title: The age that wrote the classics
history.detail: The founding corpus: the Analects' terse dialogues, the Daodejing's rhymed sententiae, the Zuo Zhuan's narrative halls — speech recorded once, then worshipped and imitated for two thousand years: vernacular of a dying dialect, grammar of an immortal language.

history.title: Shuowen Jiezi
history.detail: Xu Shen files 9,353 graphs under 540 radicals with etymological glosses — the first dictionary built to read old texts correctly, still the gateway to pre-Qin senses.

history.title: The revival that re-forged the language
history.detail: Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan's 古文运动 threw out parallel-office prose but kept the classics' grammar: after it, writing 文言 became imitating models — a learned, artificial medium by design.

history.title: Diglossia in full dress
history.detail: Ming–Qing lives in two registers: examination edicts, gazetteers and letters in 文言; novels, drama and sermons in 白话. Every literate person bilingual in one script.

history.title: The vernacular declared
history.detail: Hu Shi and Chen Duxiu demand literature in spoken language; within three years schools follow. The two-thousand-year separation ends in a decade — the moment 文言 became a foreign tongue at home.

history.title: Schools switch over
history.detail: The state mandates 国语 (spoken-based) textbooks in primary schools; 文言 retreats to universities and calligraphy scrolls, taking on its modern life as a school subject and aesthetic.

history.title: The classics return, curated
history.detail: The unified national Chinese textbook multiplies its classical selections (from the Analects to Yueyang Tower), taught with annotation technique rather than recitation: 文言 as heritage skill, quantitatively governed.

references.title: 《说文解字》
references.note: Still the etymological compass for pre-Qin senses; use with Duan Yucai's commentary (1815).

references.title: 《康熙字典》
references.note: The imperial evidence bank: sense piles ordered by citations — learn its citation logic and you can date a meaning.

references.title: 《马氏文通》
references.note: The first grammar of Classical Chinese — read its Latin-rod mistakes as a lesson in not grafting cases onto a caseless language.

references.title: 《辞源》（修订本）
references.note: The erudition dictionary: 典故 and book-senses with sources — the bridge between reading and researching.

references.title: 《切韵》
references.note: Rhyme is argument in classical scholarship: which reading, which 破音, which meaning — the 音韵 link.

references.title: 《古书句读释例》
references.note: The punctuating errors of two thousand years, catalogued — the best training ground for reading blind.
